ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethics BDSP recordings were collected under a Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board protocol (2012P001929) with a waiver of consent and used under the platform's data use agreement; the other datasets are public.
Seventeen volunteers had more true than sham calls and none the reverse (p < 0.001); a randomization test called 86.8% and 5.3% of sessions (Tables S32 and S36).
table.formatted: Seventeen volunteers had more true than sham calls and none the reverse (p < 0.001); a randomization test called 86.8% and 5.3% of sessions (Tables <ref type="table">S32</ref> and <ref type="table">S36</ref>).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Seventeen volunteers had more true than sham calls and none the reverse (p < 0.001); a randomization test called 86.8% and 5.3% of sessions (Tables S32 and S36).

Ethics approval statement:

> Ethics BDSP recordings were collected under a Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board protocol (2012P001929) with a waiver of consent and used under the platform's data use agreement; the other datasets are public.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = 0.25", Sentence = "On the 342 development recordings held locally, deleting whole commands rather than single tapered estimates in its jackknife gave a variance a median 3.9 times that expected for independent estimates and lowered false calls from 79 (23.1%) to 2 (0.6%; 95% CI, 0.1%-2.1%); with this variance, the test called 93.4% of stroke sessions (4.9 points lower; 95% CI, 0 to 12.3; 3 discordant sessions, exact McNemar p = 0.25) and none with sham labels (Tables S31, S33 and S36)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 3 columns across 1 data file.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

**Dependency-unavailable errors**
**1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to `pip install`. This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------

), class = "data.frame")

metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**`os.chdir()` in the code**
**4 scripts call `os.chdir()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with `pass`. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring an `os.chdir()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("127_fresh_rows.py", "130_fidelity_readings.py", 
"181_claassen_six.py", "test_locked_spec.py"), "os.chdir() removed" = c(1L, 
2L, 1L, 1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", "(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)", "(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

text.text: Objective: To measure how often published electroencephalographic analyses for covert command-following call patients positive without commands, and their detection of genuine responses.

This cross-sectional study applied 11 reimplemented published analyses to electroencephalograms without commands: 974 clinical electroencephalography patients and, with rules fixed, 730 new patients; 38 with prolonged disorders of consciousness; and 544 comatose patients after cardiac arrest.
Outcomes: false calls (share called positive) against a 5% benchmark, and genuine-response detection.

Results: Three of 10 command-following analyses called significantly more than 5% of clinical electroencephalography patients positive, replicated in new patients: Goldfine 2011, a spectral test, 23.3% (95% CI, 20.2%-26.6%), above its stated 5%; du Bois 2026, a criterion for entry to brain-computer interface training, 22.2% (95% CI, 19.2%-25.5%); and Guger 2018, a P300 accuracy threshold, 13.8% (95% CI, 11.5%-16.3%), near its approximate 12% chance rate (24.5% over 2 runs).
The other 7 called 0.0% to 6.9%.
After cardiac arrest: 11.5% to 27.3%.
All 3 detected genuine responses.
Identified contributors: a variance ignoring within-command dependence (Goldfine 2011), selection over configurations and times (du Bois 2026) and a permissive threshold (Guger 2018).

Goldfine 2011's command-level correction, fixed before testing, called 0.8% of new patients and 2.4% after arrest, detecting 93.4% of stroke imagery-versus-rest sessions but few between imagery types.
Interpretation: Reimplemented published analyses called up to 27% of patients positive without commands, more with repeated runs.
A positive result needs its complete call rule's false-call rate and detection at that rate; imagery-versus-rest detection may reflect task engagement, not imagery.
An unresponsive patient is asked during EEG to imagine moving a hand, and the analysis returns a positive result.

Between 15% and 25% of patients without a behavioral response show such responses, termed cognitive motor dissociation (CMD), 1, 2 which has been associated with earlier and more complete recovery. 1, 3 European and US guidelines both make weak recommendations: the European to consider task-based EEG or functional MRI in multimodal assessment, the US to allow such tests when bedside findings remain ambiguous. 4, 5 A positive result can shape prognostic counseling and decisions about life-sustaining treatment. 6 Statistical significance alone does not make a positive result trustworthy.

text.text: A widely cited motor imagery result depended on treating trials within a block as independent, 7 the binomial test of cross-validated accuracy overstates significance, 8 and publications often leave such choices unstated. 1, [9] [10] [11] A "ghost response check", running the analysis on recordings in which no task was presented, has been proposed to estimate how often current methods give false-positive results. 6 To our knowledge, it has not been carried out across published analyses or in patients.

text.text: In this cross-sectional study, we ran published EEG analyses for covert commandfollowing on recordings from patients who received no study command.
We measured how often each called patients positive, alone and over repeated runs, in clinical EEG and in coma after cardiac arrest, and whether randomizing trial order prevented it.

We then tested the analyses with excess calls on genuine responses and sham labels, identified analytical contributors to the excess and measured detection at a patient-level false-call rate targeted within each design.
This cross-sectional study used de-identified EEG recorded without study commands; reporting follows STARD 2015 and STROBE.

Clinical EEG came from the SpikeNet 2.0 corpus of the Brain Data Science Platform (BDSP), routine, epilepsymonitoring and long-term recordings from 3 institutions. 12, 13 A development set of 974 patients was analyzed first; after every analysis rule had been fixed, 730 further patients never analyzed in this study were drawn from the same corpus as a replication set (Supplementary Methods 15).

text.text: Claassen 2019 reproduces the authors' public code.

The Goldfine 2011, Chennu 2013 and Sokoliuk 2021 analyses reproduce the core statistic of a public implementation, with manual independent component analysis and visual rejection replaced by automated rules; the Goldfine 2011 statistic agreed with a translation of the public toolbox's routine to within 4 × 10 -15 on 30 random inputs, and the toolbox's variance changed none of its 79 calls on the 342 development recordings held locally.
The others were reimplemented from published descriptions; for the mindBEAGLE-type analyses, the vendor's software was not tested.
The du Bois 2026 reimplementation departs from several stated choices, among them fewer spatial filters, a coarser time step and no peak refinement (Table S4).

The covert-processing analysis 35 is reported in Supplementary Results 2. b A simplified reference: 5% for the t test plus at most 1% for the 70% threshold, which the publication places above the 99% binomial bound for 90 trials; the reference assumes independent trials, one configuration and one time point, and does not cover the search over configurations and peak times (Table S19). c More than 23% of 10 split-half predictions correct, each with a 1 in 8 chance, if the splits were independent (Table S19). d The targetword P3b against baseline, its temporal cluster test and the explicit-against-implicit contrast, the criteria the publication's positive patient met.

text.text: Each analysis's own schedule of commands or stimuli was placed on a seeded window of each recording, so every positive call was false with respect to commands.
Schedules longer than 30 minutes were also run later on longer windows where recordings held them, and Claassen 2019 on the 6 DoC channels (Supplementary Methods 18).

Per-patient rules used each patient's first windows at the published number of assessments: any of 2 recordings for Claassen 2019 (bounded with other patients' windows; Table S9B), 1,3 either of 2 sessions for du Bois 2026, either of 2 runs for Guger 2018 (with up to 7 runs reported descriptively) and 1 for the others.
text.formatted: Per-patient rules used each patient's first windows at the published number of assessments: any of 2 recordings for Claassen 2019 (bounded with other patients' windows; Table <ref type="table">S9B</ref>), 1,3 either of 2 sessions for du Bois 2026, either of 2 runs for Guger 2018 (with up to 7 runs reported descriptively) and 1 for the others.

text.text: Where a publication left a choice open, such as the cross-validation unit, each option consistent with it was run.

The primary result used the consistent option with the fewest positive calls, so primary rates are the lowest among the consistent options run; the option was chosen on each half of the patients and tested on the other; fullsample rates are reported (Table S17).
text.formatted: The primary result used the consistent option with the fewest positive calls, so primary rates are the lowest among the consistent options run; the option was chosen on each half of the patients and tested on the other; fullsample rates are reported (Table <ref type="table">S17</ref>).

text.text: This rule and corrections to 2 reimplementations were set after initial rates had been seen; results under every consistent option, the originally planned option and the chronology are in Supplementary Methods 3, 4 and 12.
The rules were then fixed and applied unchanged to the replication set.
Each analysis was also run with trial order randomized trial by trial and tested by randomization at that unit (200 draws).

Detection was measured on simulated responses added to the no-command EEG, against the published analysis sizecorrected to 5%, on healthy participants' sessions analyzed with true and shuffled labels (Supplementary Methods 7-9); Guger 2017 was also run in 47 instructed patients with acute stroke (Supplementary Methods 16).

The 3 analyses with excess calls were then run on open recordings with genuine tasks; code, sham labels and pass criteria were committed before these recordings were analyzed (Supplementary Methods 17).
The Guger 2018 rule was run on a tactile task in which 19 blind or sighted volunteers counted touches on 1 of 8 fingertips in 2 sessions each, 36 with an unattended finger as the sham label.
text.formatted: The Guger 2018 rule was run on a tactile task in which 19 blind or sighted volunteers counted touches on 1 of 8 fingertips in 2 sessions each, <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref> with an unattended finger as the sham label.

text.text: The Goldfine 2011 and du Bois 2026 rules were run on the recorded design of a stroke motor imagery dataset, 61 sessions of 23 patients alternating rest with imagery of the affected hand or of a robotic sixth finger; 37 Goldfine 2011 compared imagery with rest and du Bois 2026 the 2 imagery types, with sham labels from rest periods only (Goldfine 2011) or redrawn at random (du Bois 2026), 20 times per session.
text.formatted: The Goldfine 2011 and du Bois 2026 rules were run on the recorded design of a stroke motor imagery dataset, 61 sessions of 23 patients alternating rest with imagery of the affected hand or of a robotic sixth finger; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37</ref> Goldfine 2011 compared imagery with rest and du Bois 2026 the 2 imagery types, with sham labels from rest periods only (Goldfine 2011) or redrawn at random (du Bois 2026), 20 times per session.

text.text: On 200 development windows, a second du Bois 2026 implementation following the publication's stated choices was varied one choice at a time, and its permutation evaluation was run literally or with the configuration search repeated inside each permutation.

The Goldfine 2011 jackknife was recomputed with whole commands, rather than single tapered estimates, as the deleted unit; this variance was then fixed in code and applied unchanged to the replication and post-arrest windows, and to left-against right-hand imagery at the same post-cue time in 47 patients with acute stroke. 38 Finally, each statistic was thresholded on null recordings of its own design (command-free clinical EEG or sham labels), cross-fitted by patient, targeting a 5% chance of any false call over k assessments (1, 2, 5 or 10) under independence, and applied to genuine responses; where patients had repeated null runs, the patient-level rate was also measured directly.
text.formatted: The Goldfine 2011 jackknife was recomputed with whole commands, rather than single tapered estimates, as the deleted unit; this variance was then fixed in code and applied unchanged to the replication and post-arrest windows, and to left-against right-hand imagery at the same post-cue time in 47 patients with acute stroke. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> Finally, each statistic was thresholded on null recordings of its own design (command-free clinical EEG or sham labels), cross-fitted by patient, targeting a 5% chance of any false call over k assessments (1, 2, 5 or 10) under independence, and applied to genuine responses; where patients had repeated null runs, the patient-level rate was also measured directly.

text.text: The primary outcome was the share of patients called positive (the false-call rate), with exact Clopper-Pearson 95% CIs.
In the replication set, the 3 analyses above 5% in development were tested against 5% by one-sided exact binomial tests with Holm adjustment; no option was selected on these patients.
The other analyses were tested for rates below 10%.

Five percent was a common benchmark, not every rule's stated error rate; each rate was also compared with the rate its rule states or implies and with the same rule's rate on white noise (Table 2; Table S19).

text.text: The development set comprised 974 clinical EEG patients and the replication set 730 patients; the DoC set comprised 38 patients and the post-arrest set 544 comatose patients with a usable window, 490 of them with complete clinical data, of whom 185 (37.8%) had a good outcome (Table 1; Tables S6 and S16).
text.formatted: The development set comprised 974 clinical EEG patients and the replication set 730 patients; the DoC set comprised 38 patients and the post-arrest set 544 comatose patients with a usable window, 490 of them with complete clinical data, of whom 185 (37.8%) had a good outcome (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>; Tables <ref type="table">S6</ref> and <ref type="table">S16</ref>).

text.text: Without any study command, 3 of 10 analyses called 14% to 23% of clinical EEG patients positive.
These positive calls differ in kind: command-following (Goldfine 2011), entry to brain-computer interface training (du Bois 2026) and a discriminable response (Guger 2018) (Table 2).

text.text: All 3 analyses with excess calls detected genuine responses, so their false calls do not reflect implementations that cannot detect.
What makes a positive result interpretable is the complete patient-level rule, including the runs allowed, its false-call rate on recordings without commands and its detection of genuine responders.
The three analyses with excess calls behaved differently; only for Goldfine 2011 was a correction fixed in advance and tested in new patients.

Goldfine 2011 called no white-noise recordings, so its calls arise from properties of EEG: its jackknife treats tapered estimates within a command as independent, and on clinical EEG a variance that respects this dependence was a median 3.9 times that expected for independent estimates.
With whole commands as the jackknife unit, fixed in advance, false calls fell below 5% in new patients and after cardiac arrest while stroke imagery against rest was detected in 93.4% of sessions.

Left-against right-hand imagery at the same time after the cue was detected in few acute-stroke patients by either variance; detection against rest therefore shows task-associated EEG differences, not that the test isolates motor imagery, and the corrected variance, at 0.6% to 2.4%, may be conservative.

In our implementation, the du Bois 2026 rule compares a long task window's peak accuracy with a short baseline's; a longer window's maximum is larger by chance, and the rule called more white-noise recordings than EEG recordings.

An implementation following more of the publication's stated choices called more windows, mostly through 1 unstated choice, whether cross-validation folds respect the task blocks, and its permutation evaluation did not hold 5% with random folds.

The complete decision pathway, more than the classifier, sets the rate, and the 22% describes the advancement step as implemented, an entry criterion for training rather than the publication's full evidence of task decoding. 30 The Guger 2018 threshold would be met about 12% of the time by chance if its 10 split halves were independent, 31 close to its rates on EEG and white noise, a permissive threshold rather than a failed error guarantee: the implementation detected 95% of tactile attention sessions, and with real touch to an unattended finger it was met in 13% of runs, near that chance rate.

text.text: Implementations written independently from the same texts disagreed with ours, so a publication does not fix a single executable analysis.

Detecting healthy volunteers, the usual check that an analysis works, 25, 31 does not establish specificity: readings that detected most healthy responders also called over a quarter of shuffled sessions, and the du Bois 2026 criterion was met in about half to two thirds of stroke sessions with random labels.

text.text: Thresholds set on null recordings of each design show how much detection survives, although achieved false-call rates often exceeded their targets, by most for Guger 2018.
At thresholds for 5 assessments, the Goldfine 2011 statistic detected 95% to 100% of imagery against rest, and the du Bois 2026 and Guger 2018 statistics 2% to 30%.
The contrasts differ, so these results do not rank the methods; they show that detection must be read at the achieved false-call rate of its rule.
These are false calls without commands, not clinical false-positive rates in patients who hear commands without following them.
The original studies delivered commands to different cohorts with different preprocessing, and these results do not show that their patients were false positives.
The analyses come from publications of 2011 to 2026; whether laboratories using current, locally validated protocols have these rates was not tested.

Missed responses also cause harm, and a negative result does not exclude awareness: 2 Guger 2017 called only 1 in 5 awake patients with acute stroke positive when asked to imagine hand movements, without verified task performance.

text.text: Randomizing trial order cut false calls but lowered detection for some analyses, and its feasibility for patients was not tested.

Extending calls for standard reporting, 6, 43 we recommend that a positive EEG command-following result be reported with the false-call rate of its exact call rule on command-free recordings, including how many runs may count, and its detection rate in known responders at that false-call rate.

text.text: That rate describes chance behavior, not diagnostic specificity, which requires delivered commands in the target population.
This study has limitations.

First, the analyses were reimplemented from publications and public code, without vendor software, the original authors' review or review by an independent EEG expert; independent implementations of 2 analyses disagreed with ours, and our du Bois 2026 implementation departs from several stated choices, which moved its rate in both directions (Table S30), so the rates describe the published rules as implemented here (positive-control evidence for each, Table S23).
text.formatted: First, the analyses were reimplemented from publications and public code, without vendor software, the original authors' review or review by an independent EEG expert; independent implementations of 2 analyses disagreed with ours, and our du Bois 2026 implementation departs from several stated choices, which moved its rate in both directions (Table <ref type="table">S30</ref>), so the rates describe the published rules as implemented here (positive-control evidence for each, Table <ref type="table">S23</ref>).

text.text: Second, the real-task controls used healthy volunteers and patients after stroke, not patients with disorders of consciousness, and a tactile Braille task rather than the vendor's vibrotactile paradigm; no recordings of the original studies' patients were available, the repeated-search permutation evaluation used development windows only, and the corrected Goldfine 2011 variance was tested with commands only in stroke recordings, high against rest and low between imagery types.

Third, the choice rule and 2 corrections were set after development rates had been seen; the replication was internal to one corpus and had no background labels, and the longest schedules ran later, only where recordings held them (after arrest, 231 of 544).
Fourth, recordings without study commands may contain unannotated activation procedures, although rates were similar in awake windows without detected activation.

Fifth, the DoC set was small, had 6 channels (Claassen 2019 ran on 6 of its 19) and was exploratory; post-arrest windows were short, sedation was not recorded, and associations with outcome do not validate consciousness detection; no open EEG with delivered commands in disorders of consciousness was available.
Sixth, assembled healthy sessions lack slow drift, so leave-block-out detection is optimistic.
Seventh, repeated runs were windows of one recording.
A positive EEG command-following result should not be interpreted from the algorithm name or nominal threshold alone.

Supplementary Data S2: Supplementary tables (one worksheet per table).
Prolonged-DoC and post-arrest rates were estimated, not tested.

Only the replication tests and the frozen test of the command-level Goldfine 2011 variance (one-sided exact binomial against 5%, Holm over the replication and post-arrest sets) were confirmatory; all other analyses were exploratory, including comparisons with published cohorts that delivered commands (Supplementary Methods 16).
Real-task rates carry participant-or patient-cluster bootstrap CIs.
Analyses were run in October 2026 with Python 3.9.6 (real-task analyses, Python 3.12); code is at https://github.com/Alon-Gorenshtein/False-Positive-Calls-Covert-Command-Following-EEG.

Ethics BDSP recordings were collected under a Mass General Brigham Institutional Review Board protocol (2012P001929) with a waiver of consent and used under the platform's data use agreement; the other datasets are public.
This secondary analysis of de-identified data required no further review or consent.
